name: OONI Probe CLI / probe-engine
maintainer: Open Observatory of Network Interference (OONI) Foundation ETS
description: Go command-line client and measurement engine that runs OONI's censorship nettests (Web Connectivity, DNS consistency, HTTP invalid request line, Signal/Telegram/WhatsApp/Facebook Messenger reachability, Tor and Psiphon reachability) from a vantage point inside a network and submits results to OONI's open collector.
journalism_use_case: A reporter or local stringer runs ooniprobe from inside the affected country to generate timestamped, independently published evidence that specific news sites or messaging apps are being blocked, and what technique is doing the blocking.
language_stack: Go
deployment: self-hosted / local binary (Linux, macOS, Windows); also embedded as the engine in OONI's desktop and mobile apps
activity_evidence: GitHub API: pushed_at 2026-11-16; releases v3.31.1 published 2026-11-03 and v3.31.0 on 2026-10-22; 300 stars; archived=false. Companion ooni/probe-engine (GPL-3.0) pushed 2026-10-22.
platform_api_risk: Nettests target third-party platforms (Telegram, Signal, WhatsApp, Facebook Messenger), so endpoint or protocol changes by those vendors can cause false positives until a test is updated.
external_deps: OONI backend collector and test-helper infrastructure; Citizen Lab URL test lists; MaxMind-style GeoIP databases for ASN/country tagging.
data_flows: Measurement results are uploaded by default to OONI's collector and then published as open data, including the probe's ASN, country code, and network name; OONI documents that IP addresses are not intentionally published but measurement data is public by design.
limitations: Running probes is legally and physically risky for the operator in repressive jurisdictions; results detect anomalies, not intent, and confirming blocking usually needs corroboration across probes and time; no built-in anonymity for the person running it.

name: OONI Probe Multiplatform (Android / iOS / Desktop)
maintainer: Open Observatory of Network Interference (OONI) Foundation ETS
description: Kotlin Multiplatform rewrite of the OONI Probe end-user app for Android, iOS and desktop, giving non-technical users a tap-to-run interface over the same measurement engine used by the CLI.
journalism_use_case: Newsrooms can ask sources, correspondents or volunteer networks inside a country to install one app and run a standard test suite, producing comparable public measurements without any command-line skills.
language_stack: Kotlin (Kotlin Multiplatform / Compose)
deployment: end-user mobile and desktop app; built from source or installed from app stores
activity_evidence: GitHub API: pushed_at 2026-11-16; releases v6.3.1 published 2026-11-09, v6.3.0 on 2026-11-02, v6.2.1 on 2026-09-28; 99 stars; archived=false. Supersedes the legacy Java app ooni/probe-android, which the API reports as archived=true (pushed_at 2026-04-20).
platform_api_risk: App-store distribution is a real chokepoint: store availability in censored markets is outside OONI's control, and messaging-app nettests break when vendors change endpoints.
external_deps: OONI probe engine (Go, from probe-cli); OONI backend collector; Citizen Lab test lists; Google Play / Apple App Store for mainstream distribution.
data_flows: Results upload to OONI's collector and are republished as open data with ASN, network name and country; the app surfaces consent screens about this public publication before testing.
limitations: Still an app the user must deliberately install and run, so coverage is opportunistic and biased toward activist and technical populations; the older Android codebase is archived, so bug reports must go to the new repo.

name: OONI Explorer
maintainer: Open Observatory of Network Interference (OONI) Foundation ETS
description: Open-source web front end over OONI's measurement archive that lets anyone browse per-country, per-network and per-URL blocking evidence, inspect individual raw measurements, and link to a permanent URL for each one.
journalism_use_case: The fastest route from 'is this site blocked in country X' to a citable, linkable public measurement; the per-measurement permalinks are usable directly as sourcing in a published story.
language_stack: JavaScript (Next.js/React)
deployment: hosted public service at explorer.ooni.org; self-hostable from source
activity_evidence: GitHub API: pushed_at 2026-11-16; 95 stars; archived=false. Hosted instance https://explorer.ooni.org returned HTTP 200 when checked on 2026-11-16.
platform_api_risk: Depends entirely on the OONI measurements API (api.ooni.io) remaining available; a self-hosted copy is not useful without that backend or your own pipeline.
external_deps: OONI backend/measurements API; OONI's published measurement data store.
data_flows: Reads and displays already-public OONI measurement data; browsing is read-only and no measurement is run from the browser.
limitations: Shows anomalies and confirmed-blocking classifications, not a verdict on who ordered a block; low-coverage countries and networks can look quiet simply because nobody ran a probe there.

name: OONI backend (measurements API, collector, test helpers)
maintainer: Open Observatory of Network Interference (OONI) Foundation ETS
description: Consolidated repository for OONI's server-side infrastructure: the measurements API, the collector that receives probe submissions, bouncers and test helpers, plus sysadmin tooling, merged from the older ooni/api and ooni/pipeline repos.
journalism_use_case: Data teams query the OONI measurements API to pull structured blocking counts per country, ASN and URL over time for charts and trend reporting, instead of hand-collecting from the web UI.
language_stack: Python
deployment: self-hosted server stack; the canonical instance is OONI's own hosted API
activity_evidence: GitHub API: pushed_at 2026-11-13; 60 stars; archived=false; absorbs ooni/api, ooni/pipeline, ooni/sysadmin, collector, bouncers and test-helpers. The superseded ooni/api is archived=true (pushed_at 2023-03-16) and ooni/pipeline is dormant (pushed_at 2023-08-17). https://api.ooni.io/ returned HTTP 200 on 2026-11-16.
platform_api_risk: Journalists relying on the hosted api.ooni.io are dependent on OONI's funding and rate limits; endpoint shapes have changed across backend generations, so pinned queries can break.
external_deps: ClickHouse/PostgreSQL-class data stores and OONI's own measurement storage; the probe fleet as the data source.
data_flows: Ingests probe submissions (including ASN, network name, country, test results) and republishes them as open data via API and bulk stores.
limitations: Operationally heavy to self-host and not meant as a desktop tool; two older repos in this lineage are archived or dormant, so older tutorials point at dead code.

name: OONI Data (oonidata / oonipipeline)
maintainer: Open Observatory of Network Interference (OONI) Foundation ETS
description: CLI and 'Pipeline v5' for working with OONI measurement data in bulk - syncing raw measurements, re-processing them into analysis-ready observations, and running blocking-detection logic outside OONI's own infrastructure.
journalism_use_case: The tool to reach for when a story needs a country-wide or multi-year blocking dataset rather than individual measurements, e.g. reconstructing exactly when a set of news domains started being tampered with.
language_stack: Python
deployment: self-hosted CLI and pipeline (Docker configs and Airflow-style DAGs present in-repo)
activity_evidence: GitHub API: pushed_at 2026-11-16; 11 stars; archived=false; homepage https://docs.ooni.org/data. Root tree contains oonidata/, oonipipeline/, dags/, notebooks/.
platform_api_risk: Depends on OONI's bulk data stores and API staying accessible and schema-stable; pipeline generations (v3/v4/v5) have broken compatibility before.
external_deps: OONI measurement archive (bulk object storage), ClickHouse-class analytics store for the pipeline, Python 3 toolchain.
data_flows: Pulls already-public OONI measurements down to local or cloud storage and derives observation tables; no new measurement traffic is generated.
limitations: GitHub reports no licence for this repo because the root has no LICENSE file - the BSD-3-Clause text sits in the oonidata/ and oonipipeline/ subpackages, so licence clarity at the repo level is poor. Full-corpus processing needs real storage and compute; analyst tooling, not a newsroom app.

name: Citizen Lab URL test lists
maintainer: The Citizen Lab, University of Toronto (community-contributed)
description: Curated, per-country and global CSV lists of URLs intended for censorship testing, categorised by topic (news media, human rights, LGBTQ, political criticism and so on), with scripts for validation.
journalism_use_case: Defines what gets tested, so a newsroom can check whether the outlets it cares about are even in the list for a country - and submit them if not - before citing OONI coverage as evidence of press blocking.
language_stack: CSV data with Python helper scripts
deployment: git clone / direct CSV download; consumed automatically by OONI Probe
activity_evidence: GitHub API: pushed_at 2026-11-04; 554 stars; archived=false; GitHub reports no SPDX licence (no LICENSE file), but the README's License section links to the CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 legalcode and summary pages.
platform_api_risk: None directly; the risk is editorial - list composition drives what censorship is visible in downstream datasets.
external_deps: None to read the data; OONI's probe tooling to act on it.
data_flows: Static public data in git; no measurement or personal data involved.
limitations: The NonCommercial clause in CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 is a genuine problem for commercial newsrooms that want to redistribute or build products on the lists - legal review is warranted; there is no LICENSE file, only a README statement. Coverage is uneven by country and depends on volunteer submissions, so absence of an outlet is not evidence it is unblocked.

name: IODA (Internet Outage Detection and Analysis)
maintainer: Internet Intelligence Lab, Georgia Institute of Technology (originally CAIDA / UC San Diego)
description: Near-real-time Internet connectivity monitoring platform that fuses three independent signals - BGP routing data from RouteViews and RIPE RIS, Trinocular-style ICMP active probing, and network-telescope background radiation - into per-country and per-ASN connectivity timelines, with a public dashboard and REST API.
journalism_use_case: The standard first stop for confirming and timestamping a national or regional internet shutdown, because agreement across three unrelated signals is hard to explain away as a measurement artefact.
language_stack: JavaScript front end (ioda-ui); PHP/Symfony API (ioda-api); Python and C supporting components (chocolatine, watchtower-sentry, libbgpstream, libtimeseries, corsaro3)
deployment: hosted public dashboard and API operated by Georgia Tech; components are source-available for self-hosting but not packaged for easy reuse
activity_evidence: GitHub API: InetIntel/ioda-ui pushed_at 2026-11-02, InetIntel/ioda-api pushed_at 2026-10-21, InetIntel/watchtower-sentry pushed_at 2026-10-19, InetIntel/chocolatine (S-ARIMA alert detection) pushed_at 2025-05-26; none archived. The older CAIDA/ioda-ui mirror is stale (pushed_at 2023-07-14). https://ioda.inetintel.cc.gatech.edu/ returned HTTP 200 on 2026-11-16.
platform_api_risk: Signals are second-hand: BGP feeds (RouteViews, RIPE RIS) and the telescope are operated by others, and the hosted API is a single academic-funded service with no commercial SLA.
external_deps: RouteViews and RIPE RIS BGP collectors; ICMP-reachable address space for active probing; a darknet/telescope feed; Kafka and time-series storage; libbgpstream, libtimeseries, libipmeta.
data_flows: Aggregates network-level public measurement data to country/region/ASN granularity; it observes reachability of address space, not individuals or content.
limitations: The LICENSE text read on both the CAIDA and InetIntel copies grants use for academic research and education without fee and directs other uses to contact the university - so despite public code this is source-available, not OSI open source, and a commercial newsroom redeploying it should get permission. Signals show loss of reachability, not cause: a shutdown, a cut cable and a power failure can look alike, and sub-national granularity is coarse.

name: PyBGPStream / libbgpstream
maintainer: CAIDA, UC San Diego; actively forked and maintained by Georgia Tech's Internet Intelligence Lab
description: C library and Python bindings for streaming and analysing historical and live BGP routing data from RouteViews, RIPE RIS and similar collectors, including route withdrawals and prefix visibility over time.
journalism_use_case: Lets a data journalist independently reconstruct which ASNs withdrew which prefixes, and at what minute, during a shutdown - the evidence that distinguishes an operator-executed disconnection from a transit failure.
language_stack: C with Python bindings
deployment: self-hosted library; pulls data from public BGP collector archives
activity_evidence: GitHub API: CAIDA/pybgpstream pushed_at 2026-07-06, 45 stars, archived=false, latest release v2.0.4 published 2024-02-20. The C client library has moved forward under InetIntel/libbgpstream (BSD-2-Clause, pushed_at 2026-07-07); CAIDA/bgpstream itself is dormant (pushed_at 2019-12-19).
platform_api_risk: Entirely dependent on third-party BGP collector archives (RouteViews, RIPE RIS) remaining public and on their file formats; broker endpoints have changed between versions.
external_deps: libbgpstream and its C build chain (wandio, librdkafka), RouteViews/RIPE RIS MRT archives.
data_flows: Reads public routing-table and update archives; no probing and no user data.
limitations: Build and dependency setup is genuinely fiddly and release cadence is slow (last tagged release 2024); BGP shows control-plane intent, so routes can stay announced while the data plane is blocked, and vice versa. Maintenance is split between the CAIDA and InetIntel lineages, a confusing provenance picture.

name: Censored Planet data analysis pipeline
maintainer: Censored Planet Observatory, University of Michigan (pipeline originally from Jigsaw-Code)
description: Pipeline that ingests the multi-terabyte raw output of the Censored Planet Observatory's remote-measurement techniques (Satellite/Iris DNS and Hyperquack/Quack-style TCP, HTTP and TLS probing) and turns it into queryable BigQuery tables.
journalism_use_case: Underpins global, longitudinal blocking comparisons across ~200 countries without anyone having to run a probe inside a censored network, which matters when in-country testing is unsafe.
language_stack: Python (Apache Beam / Google Cloud Dataflow, BigQuery)
deployment: requires a dedicated Google Cloud project; the README explicitly says running it yourself is not recommended and the code is published mainly for transparency
activity_evidence: GitHub API: pushed_at 2025-06-29; 20 stars; archived=false. README confirms it processes Censored Planet Observatory data and still carries a Jigsaw-Code build badge. https://data.censoredplanet.org/ returned HTTP 200 on 2026-11-16 while https://censoredplanet.org/data returned 404.
platform_api_risk: Hard dependency on Google Cloud (Dataflow, BigQuery, GCS); there is no vendor-neutral path, which also means real cost exposure.
external_deps: Google Cloud Platform; Censored Planet raw data releases; censoredplanet/assets-censoredplanet (blockpage fingerprints).
data_flows: Processes already-published remote-measurement data about network behaviour; the measurement technique probes infrastructure rather than user devices.
limitations: Not runnable by a newsroom in practice - treat the published BigQuery tables and raw releases as the deliverable and this repo as methodological documentation. Remote-measurement techniques infer blocking from side channels, so they are more prone to false positives than in-country probes. Last push mid-2025.

name: CenAlert
description: Research implementation of an alerting system that watches country- and topic-level signals (including Google Trends) to flag likely new censorship events, with a dashboard and Slack notification path.
journalism_use_case: Points toward an early-warning tripwire - being told a country may have started censoring a topic before a story breaks - rather than confirming a block after the fact.
language_stack: Python 3.8-3.12 with shell configuration
deployment: self-hosted scripts; needs credentials provisioned before first run
activity_evidence: GitHub API: pushed_at 2026-10-29, archived=false, 3 stars; latest default-branch commit 2026-04-06 ('Pushing CenAlert dashboard implementation code'). Companion censoredplanet/cenalert-paper (GPL-3.0) pushed 2026-04-06.
platform_api_risk: High and explicit: the README states CenAlert requires a Google Trends API key and a Slack token, so it is hostage to Google's unofficial trends access and quota and to Slack's API. Note that GeneralMills/pytrends, the usual Google Trends client, was archived 2024-08.
external_deps: Google Trends access, Slack token, Python 3.8-3.12, per-topic/per-country configuration in bin/config.sh.
data_flows: Consumes aggregate public search-interest signals and censorship measurement data and pushes alerts to a Slack workspace; no individual-level data.
limitations: A paper-accompanying prototype with almost no external users, thin documentation, and no packaging; alerts are probabilistic hints that need verification against OONI or IODA before publication. The two-key requirement is a practical barrier.

name: M-Lab NDT server, ndt7 client and MSAK
description: M-Lab's open measurement stack: the ndt5/ndt7 server with Prometheus integration, reference Go client, and MSAK ('Measurements Swiss Army Knife') for multi-stream throughput and latency tests, all feeding M-Lab's openly published dataset.
journalism_use_case: Evidence for throttling and degradation stories - the slow-lane variant of a shutdown, where connectivity technically persists but collapses in throughput - and for long-run comparisons of network performance by ISP and region.
language_stack: Go (Docker-native server)
deployment: self-hosted server/client, plus M-Lab's global hosted measurement platform and public dataset
activity_evidence: GitHub API: m-lab/ndt-server pushed_at 2026-10-15, release v0.26.1 published 2026-10-15 and v0.26.0 on 2026-10-06, 137 stars, archived=false; m-lab/msak pushed_at 2026-11-14 (last release v0.4.7 on 2024-10-07), Apache-2.0, 32 stars; m-lab/ndt7-client-go pushed_at 2026-09-22, Apache-2.0, 55 stars.
platform_api_risk: Low on the code side; the hosted platform and its BigQuery dataset are a single-provider dependency, and historical test families (ndt5 vs ndt7) are not directly comparable.
external_deps: Go toolchain, Docker, Prometheus for metrics; M-Lab's server fleet and BigQuery dataset for the hosted data.
data_flows: Tests measure the client's own connection; M-Lab publishes results openly including truncated client IP and ASN, a documented privacy trade-off journalists should disclose when citing it.
limitations: This is performance measurement, not censorship detection - it will not tell you a site is blocked, only that a path is degraded, and attributing degradation to deliberate throttling needs corroboration. MSAK's last tagged release is from 2024.

name: RIPE Atlas tooling (Magellan CLI, Cousteau, Sagan)
description: Official RIPE Atlas client suite: the ripe-atlas command-line tool (Magellan) for creating and streaming measurements, Cousteau as the Python API client, and Sagan as the result-parsing library, driving a global fleet of thousands of hardware and software probes.
journalism_use_case: Lets a reporter schedule pings, traceroutes, DNS and TLS measurements from probes inside a specific country or ASN during an unfolding shutdown, and watch probe disconnections as an independent outage signal.
language_stack: Python
deployment: local CLI/library against the hosted RIPE Atlas API and probe network
activity_evidence: GitHub API: ripe-atlas-tools pushed_at 2026-10-22, 218 stars, archived=false, latest release v3.2.0 published 2025-09-25; ripe-atlas-cousteau pushed_at 2026-10-22 (GPL-3.0, 68 stars, last release v2.0.0 on 2023-01-20); ripe-atlas-sagan pushed_at 2026-06-03 (GPL-3.0, 52 stars).
platform_api_risk: Significant: creating measurements requires a RIPE Atlas API key and spends 'credits' earned by hosting a probe, and RIPE NCC controls quotas, fair-use rules and probe availability. Terms changes directly affect what a newsroom can run.
external_deps: RIPE Atlas REST API and credit system; the volunteer-hosted probe fleet; Python 3 environment.
data_flows: Measurements are initiated by you from third-party probes and, by default, results are published publicly in RIPE Atlas; probe hosts' approximate locations and ASNs are public.
limitations: Probe coverage is thin and skewed in exactly the countries that matter most for shutdown reporting, so a country may have too few probes to say anything; credits are a real throttle on sustained measurement, and an absent probe is not evidence of an outage. Cousteau's last tagged release is from 2023.

name: Internet Health Report (IHR)
maintainer: IIJ Research Lab / Internet Health Report project
description: Open-source analysis stack and public dashboard that derives network-health indicators from RIPE Atlas and BGP data - AS interdependency ('hegemony'), delay and forwarding anomalies, link congestion - plus tools like disco that infer outages from mass RIPE Atlas probe disconnections.
journalism_use_case: Useful for the attribution half of a shutdown story: showing which upstream AS a country depends on, and therefore which operator or transit provider is the chokepoint when connectivity drops.
language_stack: Vue.js front end; Python analysis components (raclette, ashash, disco, ip2asn, abondance client, kafka-toolbox)
deployment: hosted public dashboard and API at ihr.iijlab.net; components self-hostable
activity_evidence: GitHub API: ihr-website pushed_at 2026-10-23 (GPL-3.0, 93 stars, archived=false); org active with raclette pushed 2026-11-12 and kafka-toolbox 2026-11-12. Supporting pieces: abondance Python client (GPL-3.0, pushed 2024-05-23), disco 'Outage detection using RIPE Atlas probe disconnections' (GPL-3.0, pushed 2022-04-11), ashash (GPL-3.0, 2022-05-10). The old API repo ihr-django is archived=true (pushed 2025-01-21).
platform_api_risk: Inherits RIPE Atlas and BGP collector dependencies; the hosted API has already been through one generation change (ihr-django archived), so pinned integrations can break.
external_deps: RIPE Atlas measurement results, RouteViews/RIPE RIS BGP data, Kafka cluster, Python analysis stack.
data_flows: Processes public network measurement and routing data into aggregate per-AS and per-country indicators; no end-user data.
limitations: A research codebase rather than a product: several analysis components (disco, ashash) untouched since 2022, documentation uneven, and the indicators need expert interpretation - AS hegemony is not a plain-language finding. Best used via the hosted dashboard.

name: Internet Society Pulse
description: Hosted public dashboard aggregating third-party measurement signals (including OONI, IODA, Google transparency data and M-Lab) into country-level internet resilience, shutdown and market-concentration views, with a public data repository alongside it.
journalism_use_case: A no-code entry point for a reporter who needs a credible country shutdown timeline and citable summary figures in minutes, without running or interpreting raw measurements.
language_stack: not applicable (hosted web platform; the public repo holds data/cached content, not the dashboard code)
deployment: hosted SaaS dashboard only; no self-hosting path
activity_evidence: GitHub API: InternetSociety/pulse-data pushed_at 2026-09-19, archived=false, no SPDX licence detected, root tree contains only README.md and locally_cached_content - i.e. not the dashboard source. No public repository for the Pulse application itself was found in the InternetSociety org listing. https://pulse.internetsociety.org/ returned HTTP 200 on 2026-11-16.
platform_api_risk: Entirely dependent on the Internet Society continuing to operate the service and on its upstream providers' APIs; no code means no fork path if it is discontinued or changes methodology.
external_deps: Upstream measurement providers (OONI, IODA, M-Lab and others) and their APIs.
data_flows: Presents aggregated public measurement data; visiting the dashboard sends no measurement traffic of your own.
limitations: Classified adjacent rather than open source: the dashboard's code is not public and the one public repo carries no licence, so reuse terms are unverified. Figures are derived from other people's measurements, so for any contested claim cite the underlying OONI or IODA evidence.

name: changedetection.io
description: Self-hosted web page change detection and notification service with CSS/XPath/JSON selectors, text and visual diffing, optional real-browser fetching, and over 85 notification targets. The same codebase also backs a paid hosted subscription that funds development.
journalism_use_case: Watch specific regions of agency pages, FOIA logs, press-release indexes or policy PDFs and get an email/Slack/Discord alert with a diff when the wording quietly changes.
language_stack: Python (Flask); Docker images; optional Playwright/Puppeteer/Selenium browser fetchers
deployment: self-hosted (pip or Docker/docker-compose); vendor-hosted SaaS also offered
activity_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-16: pushed_at 2026-11-16T08:48:22Z, 35,839 stars, not archived; latest release 0.70.3 published 2026-11-09; HEAD commits dated 2026-11-16.
platform_api_risk: Low for core HTTP fetching; the browser-based fetchers track fast-moving Chromium/Playwright/Puppeteer releases, and notification delivery depends on third-party services (Apprise targets, SMTP).
external_deps: Apprise for notifications; optional Playwright/Puppeteer/Selenium + Chromium container for JS-heavy pages; Docker
data_flows: Snapshots and diffs stored locally in the self-hosted instance; notification payloads (which can include page text) are sent to whichever third-party channel is configured.
limitations: Per-URL watch model with no built-in editorial triage/annotation workflow; JS-heavy or bot-protected government portals need the browser fetcher and may still block; frequent releases mean upgrade churn.

name: urlwatch
description: Long-running command-line tool that watches URLs (and shell command output) defined in a YAML jobs file, applies filters to strip boilerplate, and reports unified diffs through pluggable reporters. It is the ancestor of several later monitoring tools.
journalism_use_case: Script a reproducible watchlist of statute, regulation or guidance pages in version control, and receive diffs by email, Slack, Matrix or stdout when an official page is edited.
language_stack: Python; YAML job/filter configuration
deployment: self-hosted / local CLI, usually driven by cron or systemd timers
activity_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-16: pushed_at 2026-07-10T08:56:34Z, 3,148 stars, 85 open issues, not archived; HEAD commits dated 2026-07-09/10. The releases/latest endpoint returned 404, so release cadence was not confirmed.
platform_api_risk: Low; plain HTTP fetching plus optional Playwright 'browser' jobs, so JS rendering depends on the browser stack rather than any vendor API.
external_deps: Python 3; optional Playwright for browser jobs; optional jq/html2text/beautifulsoup-style filters; reporter-specific credentials
data_flows: Snapshot cache and diffs stay on the local machine; only the configured reporter transmits content off-box.
limitations: CLI/text-first with no web UI or multi-user triage; no built-in archiving of the captured snapshot as evidence; four-month gap since last push at time of checking.

name: webchanges
description: Actively maintained Python tool, derived from urlwatch, that checks web content (including PDFs, images and command output) for changes and reports rich HTML diffs, with optional AI-generated change summaries.
journalism_use_case: Monitor official documents and dashboards that urlwatch handles poorly (PDF text, images, JSON APIs) and receive readable HTML diffs of what an agency altered.
language_stack: Python; YAML job configuration
deployment: self-hosted / local CLI via pip, scheduled by cron or Task Scheduler
activity_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-16: pushed_at 2026-11-15T08:26:43Z, 50 stars, 6 open issues, not archived. LICENSE.md read 2026-11-16 states 'The MIT License (MIT) Copyright (c) 2020- Mike Borsetti' plus a redistribution notice for urlwatch 2.21 under BSD-3-Clause terms.
platform_api_risk: Optional AI summarisation sends page content to an external LLM provider, which is a configuration-time choice; otherwise plain HTTP plus optional Playwright.
external_deps: Python 3; optional Playwright/Chromium; optional LLM API key for AI summaries; reporter credentials
data_flows: Snapshots and diffs held locally; content leaves the machine only via configured reporters or, if enabled, the AI summarisation provider.
limitations: Effectively a single-maintainer project with a small user base; no web UI or collaborative review; the AI summary feature introduces a third-party data-sharing decision newsrooms should review before use on sensitive beats.

name: Klaxon (self-hosted, The Marshall Project)
description: Rails web app, built and used in The Marshall Project newsroom, that lets non-technical reporters 'bookmark' a selected portion of a page with a bookmarklet and be emailed (or Slack/Discord-notified) when that section changes. Its README states the self-hosted version remains free and open source but is no longer supported for individual users, who are pointed at Klaxon Cloud.
journalism_use_case: Give reporters without command-line skills a point-and-click way to watch FOIA disclosure logs, court dockets and agency pages and get alerted to newsworthy edits.
language_stack: Ruby on Rails + PostgreSQL (GitHub reports primary language SCSS); Heroku or Docker deployment
deployment: self-hosted; one-click Heroku deploy is the documented path, with Docker and Ubuntu install guides also present
activity_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-16: pushed_at 2026-11-16T10:03:32Z, 683 stars, not archived; latest release v0.7.0 published 2026-03-09. HEAD commits dated 2026-11-11 are dependency bumps (Rails 8.1.4.1), i.e. upkeep rather than feature work. newsklaxon.org fetched 2026-11-16 and live.
platform_api_risk: Deployment-platform rather than API risk: the documented path assumes Heroku (README notes Heroku's free tier is gone and budgets roughly $10/month plus SendGrid and Postgres add-ons).
external_deps: Heroku (or self-managed Docker/Linux host), PostgreSQL, SendGrid or other SMTP, optional Slack/Discord webhooks
data_flows: Watch list, snapshots and diffs live in the newsroom's own Postgres instance; alert emails route through the configured mail provider.
limitations: README explicitly warns it 'may break unexpectedly' and may miss a change or fail to send mail; individual-user support discontinued; recent repo activity is dependency maintenance, not development.

name: Klaxon Cloud (MuckRock/DocumentCloud Add-On)
description: Rebuild of Klaxon as a DocumentCloud Add-On: a Python add-on script runs each check as a DocumentCloud Add-On Run in GitHub Actions, while a separate monorepo holds the browser extension and SvelteKit site used to pick the page region to watch. Per the Klaxon-Cloud README each detected change is backed by an Internet Archive snapshot and a visual diff.
journalism_use_case: Lets a reporter with only a DocumentCloud account monitor web pages for newsworthy edits without running a server, with an Internet Archive snapshot attached as evidence of the before-and-after.
language_stack: Python add-on script; TypeScript/Svelte 5 + Vite extension and SvelteKit site on Cloudflare Workers
deployment: hosted - runs on DocumentCloud's Add-On platform (scheduling and storage via DocumentCloud Add-On Events/Runs executed in GitHub Actions); source public for inspection or forking

platform_api_risk: High coupling to one platform stack: DocumentCloud accounts and Add-On Events, GitHub Actions as the execution runtime, Cloudflare Workers for the site, Chrome Web Store/Firefox review for the extension, and the Internet Archive save endpoint for snapshots.

name: EDGI web-monitoring-db
description: Rails HTTP API that stores versions of tracked pages, records diffs between them, and lets analysts annotate and prioritise changes; it is the database tier of EDGI's Website Monitoring ('Scanner') system, paired with web-monitoring-ui for human review. EDGI runs it as the backend of the Federal Environmental Web Tracker.
journalism_use_case: Provides the newsroom-grade pipeline for monitoring thousands of government pages at once, with an annotation workflow so analysts can separate boilerplate churn from substantive policy rewording before it reaches reporters.
language_stack: Ruby on Rails + PostgreSQL; paired React UI (web-monitoring-ui) and Python tooling (web-monitoring-processing)
deployment: self-hosted server stack (API + database + UI + import pipeline); EDGI operates a public instance

Companions same day: web-monitoring-ui pushed 2026-11-06 (GPL-3.0), web-monitoring-processing pushed 2026-11-16 (GPL-3.0), web-monitoring-ops pushed 2026-11-13, docs repo pushed 2026-07-28 (CC-BY-SA-4.0). The older web-monitoring-versionista-scraper repo is archived.
platform_api_risk: Snapshot supply depends on the Internet Archive Wayback Machine (EDGI's public tracker relies on daily IA captures), so IA availability, rate limits and crawl coverage are upstream dependencies.
external_deps: PostgreSQL, Redis/Sidekiq-style job processing, Internet Archive Wayback as a version source, web-monitoring-diff for diffing, web-monitoring-ui for review

name: EDGI web-monitoring-diff
description: Python library plus optional HTTP server providing a suite of diff algorithms tuned for web content - HTML-aware, text, source and link diffs - originally built for EDGI's web monitoring work and since adopted by other organisations.
journalism_use_case: Produces the side-by-side and inline HTML diffs that let a reporter see exactly which sentences, links or data tables were removed from an official page between two archived captures.
language_stack: Python (Tornado-based diff server); C extension for some diff routines
deployment: library embedded in your own code, or self-hosted HTTP diff service (Docker available)

name: wayback (Python client for the Internet Archive Wayback Machine)
description: Python API client for the Internet Archive Wayback Machine that searches CDX capture indexes and retrieves the raw archived content of specific mementos, built and maintained by EDGI for its government-website monitoring pipeline.
journalism_use_case: Enumerate every archived capture of a government URL and pull the exact bytes of two dates to prove what a page said before and after an edit, without screen-scraping the Wayback web interface.
language_stack: Python
deployment: library installed via pip into your own scripts or pipeline
activity_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-16: pushed_at 2026-11-06T21:30:02Z, BSD-3-Clause confirmed via the licence endpoint (LICENSE at main), 94 stars, not archived.
platform_api_risk: High dependency on Internet Archive services: the CDX/memento endpoints are undocumented-to-semi-documented, rate limited, occasionally unavailable, and subject to IA's terms and exclusion policies, all of which can break or blank out a monitoring run.
external_deps: Internet Archive Wayback Machine CDX and memento endpoints; Python 3; requests-style HTTP stack
data_flows: Sends the URLs you query to the Internet Archive and pulls archived content back; your query pattern is visible to IA.
limitations: Only as good as IA's crawl coverage - pages never captured, captured rarely, or excluded cannot be reconstructed; no diffing, scheduling or alerting of its own.

name: ArchiveBox
description: Self-hosted web archiving application that takes URLs from feeds, bookmarks, browser history or the CLI and saves multiple renditions of each page - HTML, screenshot, PDF, WARC, media and more - into a browsable local archive with a web UI.
journalism_use_case: Build your own tamper-evident archive of official pages and documents on a schedule, so that when an agency rewrites or deletes a page you hold dated local copies rather than depending on a third-party archive.
language_stack: Python (Django) with many external extractor binaries; Docker images
deployment: self-hosted via pip, Docker or docker-compose; local web UI plus CLI

limitations: Not a change-detection tool - it captures and preserves, and diffing between snapshots is not its job; heavy dependency surface and long-running release-candidate versions; archive size grows quickly.

name: browsertrix-crawler
description: Browser-based archival crawler that runs in a single Docker container and produces high-fidelity WARC/WACZ captures of JavaScript-heavy sites, including behaviours that scroll, expand and play content during capture. It is the crawler engine behind Webrecorder's hosted Browsertrix service.
journalism_use_case: Capture modern government portals, dashboards and interactive document viewers faithfully enough that the archived copy still behaves like the live page when a disputed change is later examined.

activity_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-16: pushed_at 2026-11-14T19:26:24Z, AGPL-3.0, 1,197 stars, 152 open issues, not archived; latest release v1.15.4 published 2026-11-11. Companion webrecorder/browsertrix pushed 2026-11-14 (AGPL-3.0).

limitations: No change detection or alerting - it is capture infrastructure; AGPL-3.0 has network-service implications if you expose a modified version; resource-hungry and requires Docker ops familiarity.

name: Scoop

name: diffengine
maintainer: Documenting the Now (DocNow); originally Ed Summers

journalism_use_case: The reference design for publicly surfacing stealth edits to anything with a feed - news sites, ministry press-release feeds, agency blogs - with an Internet Archive snapshot attached to each detected change.

Written for the pre-2023 Twitter API; free write access to X/Twitter has since been restricted, and the README describes Twitter or email delivery, so social posting should be assumed broken without rework. Also depends on the Internet Archive save endpoint and on GeckoDriver/Selenium versions that have moved on.

limitations: Unmaintained since 2020 with broken-by-default social integration and aged browser-automation dependencies; only monitors content reachable through a feed.
